items.caption: A complementary pair, frozen at 35° and 55°
items.text: The two acute angles of a right triangle always add to 90°, so each is the other’s complement. The side opposite one of them is the side adjacent to the other — which is why the sine of 35° and the cosine of 55° are the same number, and why every co-function pair works the same way.

items.caption: The arc and the radius, same length
items.text: Both radii and the arc between them carry a single tick, because all three are the same length. That is the entire definition: swing the radius round until the arc it sweeps matches it, and the angle you have opened is one radian — about 57.3°, on a circle of any size.

items.caption: Radius, angle, arc
items.text: Because the angle is already a ratio of two lengths, multiplying it by the radius gives back a length directly. Nothing is converted and no constant appears — which is exactly what the degree version of the same formula cannot do.

items.caption: The slice against the whole
items.text: The shaded wedge occupies the same share of the disc that θ occupies of a full turn. Multiply that share by the area of the whole circle and the π cancels, which is where the compact form of the sector-area formula comes from.

items.caption: Complementary 35° + 55°; supplementary 110° + 70°

items.caption: y = sin x repeats every 2π
items.text: Any horizontal line between −1 and 1 cuts this wave twice in every period, and the cuts recur every 2π in both directions: that is why one solution always brings infinitely many with it, and why the general solution carries an integer n. The marker at 60° is one of the crossings for the line y = √3/2. Follow the wave through several periods on the

items.text: Both hover boxes show the same y-coordinate, 1/2: the two points sit at the same height on opposite sides of the y-axis, one at the reference angle 30° in Quadrant I and one at 180° − 30° in Quadrant II. items.caption: y = tan x: one crossing per branch
items.text: Every branch climbs through all real values exactly once, so a horizontal line at any height a meets the curve once per branch and the branches are π apart: tan x = a has exactly one solution per period of π, whatever a is. The marker at 60° is the crossing for a = √3. Pick any height and count the crossings on the

items.caption: Same line, same interval, twice the crossings
items.text: Doubling the angle squeezes two full cycles into the interval that held one, so the same horizontal line is crossed twice as often. The four marked points are exactly the four solutions listed above — and the two a hurried solver finds are only the first half of them.

items.caption: sin 50° ≈ 0.766, the vertical leg
items.text: On the unit circle the hypotenuse is the radius, 1, so opposite over hypotenuse collapses to the length of the blue vertical leg: at 50° it is 0.766, the highlighted first entry of the value row. The leg can never be longer than the radius, which is why the ratio never leaves [−1, 1]. Drag the point and watch the leg and the entry change together on the

items.text: Opposite over adjacent is the blue leg divided by the red one, 0.766/0.643 ≈ 1.192, and that ratio is exactly the slope of the radius line. Near 90° the red leg shrinks toward zero and the ratio grows without bound, which is why the table prints Undefined there. items.text: At 30° the blue leg is exactly half the radius, so hypotenuse over opposite is exactly 2, the highlighted entry. items.caption: sec 60° = 2, hypotenuse over adjacent
items.text: At 60° the red leg is half the radius, so hypotenuse over adjacent is exactly 2. The picture is the cosecant one with the roles of the legs exchanged: the same bound |sec θ| ≥ 1, and Undefined where the red leg vanishes at 90° and 270°. items.caption: cot 45° = 1, adjacent over opposite
items.text: At 45° the two legs are equal, so adjacent over opposite is exactly 1, and so is its reciprocal in the tangent column beside it. Away from 45° the two columns are reciprocals of each other, cotangent falling as tangent rises, with Undefined where the blue leg vanishes at 0° and 180°. items.caption: Six functions, two patterns
items.text: The dashed lines mark where each function is undefined. Tangent and secant break in exactly the same places, because both divide by cosine; cotangent and cosecant break in the same places as each other, because both divide by sine. Sine and cosine divide by nothing and never break.

items.secTitle: Finding All Function Values from One Known Value
items.caption: From one value to all six
items.text: The Pythagorean identity settles how big the second value is; the quadrant settles whether it is positive or negative. Once both are known the remaining four are reciprocals and a quotient away — and without the quadrant, half of them would have the wrong sign.

items.caption: y = sin x, marker at 60°
items.text: The wave starts at the origin, peaks at 1 a quarter of the way through the cycle, crosses zero at the half, bottoms at −1 at three quarters and closes the cycle at 2π; the marker at 60° reads √3/2 ≈ 0.866. Nothing on the curve leaves the band between −1 and 1. Slide the marker through a full period on the

items.caption: y = cos x, marker at 60°
items.text: The same wave, started from its maximum: cos 0 = 1, zero at π/2, minimum at π. The marker at 60° reads exactly 1/2, and the whole curve is the sine curve pushed π/2 to the left. Compare the two curves at the same marker on the

items.caption: y = tan x, asymptotes π apart
items.text: Each branch climbs from −∞ to +∞ between two vertical asymptotes, which stand exactly where the cosine is zero; the marker at 60° reads √3 ≈ 1.732. The branches repeat every π, half the period of sine and cosine, and there is no maximum or minimum anywhere. Approach an asymptote with the marker on the

items.secTitle: Graphs of Cosecant, Secant, and Cotangent
items.caption: y = csc x, y = sec x, y = cot x at 60°
items.text: The cosecant and secant curves are U-shaped branches that open away from the axis, each asymptote standing at a zero of the function underneath it, and each branch turning around where that function peaks; the cotangent falls where the tangent climbs and vanishes where the tangent is undefined. At 60° the three markers read 1.155, 2 and 0.577. See each curve drawn over its parent on the

items.caption: One wave, four parameters
items.text: Each parameter owns one feature and leaves the others alone. A sets the distance from the midline to a peak, B sets how much horizontal room one cycle takes, C slides the cycle sideways, and D raises or lowers the line the wave oscillates about.

items.caption: A = 1 against A = 3
items.text: Both waves cross zero at the same places and close a cycle over the same interval — only the height changes. Tripling A triples the distance from the midline to the peak and moves nothing else.

items.caption: B = 1 against B = 2
items.text: Doubling B halves the horizontal room one cycle needs, so two complete cycles now fit where one did. The height is untouched: both waves still run between −1 and 1.

items.caption: Where the cycle starts
items.text: The argument 2x − π vanishes at x = π/2, so that is where the standard cycle begins — half of π, not π. Reading C straight off as the shift is the common error.

items.caption: D = 0 against D = 2
items.text: Adding 2 lifts the midline from y = 0 to y = 2 and carries the whole wave with it. The bracket from midline to peak is the same length in both panels: D does not touch the amplitude.

items.secTitle: Determining the Equation from a Graph
items.caption: Five readings, in order
items.text: The order is forced. Maximum and minimum come first because everything else is built from them: their average is the midline, half their difference is the amplitude, and only then does the horizontal length of one cycle give B.

items.secTitle: Graphing by Hand: The Key-Point Method
items.caption: One period, four equal parts
items.text: Dividing a period into quarters puts five points on the curve at heights midline, maximum, midline, minimum, midline. Those five fix the shape; the curve is drawn through them freehand.

items.caption: Two points, or everything between them
items.text: The equation is answered by the two marked crossings and nothing else. The inequality is answered by the whole shaded stretch between them — and it is continuity that guarantees no gaps appear inside, since the curve cannot get back below the line without crossing it again.

items.caption: y = sin x: where the curve sits above a level
items.text: Where the wave lies above a chosen height is an interval, not a point: for the level 1/2 the curve is above it from 30° to 150° and then again one period later, and below it everywhere else in the cycle. The marker at 60° sits inside that interval, at height 0.866. Move the marker along the curve and watch it enter and leave the solution set on the

items.caption: Arc on the left, band on the right
items.text: Both panels answer sin x ≥ √2/2 and both give π/4 and 3π/4. On the circle the answer is the arc whose points sit above the line; under the curve it is the interval where the graph sits above the same height. Picking a method is a matter of which picture you find quicker to read.

items.caption: Two bounds, one answer
items.text: Each bound has its own solution set, drawn as a bar under the curve. The compound inequality is satisfied only where the two bars overlap, which here breaks the answer into two separate intervals rather than one.

items.secTitle: Domain Considerations for Reciprocal and Quotient Functions
items.caption: y = sec x: asymptotes at every zero of cosine
items.text: The upward branches of the secant curve sit only where the cosine is positive and never dip below 1, so sec x ≥ 2 is solved on those branches alone, between the asymptotes at 90° and 270° that must be excluded from any solution set. The marker at 60° reads exactly 2, an endpoint of the answer. Trace a branch out to its asymptote on the

items.caption: One line, four crossings
items.text: A horizontal line meets the full sine curve at infinitely many points, four of them in the stretch drawn here. Inside the shaded interval it meets the curve exactly once — which is what makes an inverse possible there and nowhere wider.

items.caption: Sine and arcsine across y = x
items.text: Arcsine is not a new curve. It is the restricted sine with its two coordinates exchanged, which is what reflecting across the dashed line does. The endpoint at (π/2, 1) becomes (1, π/2).

items.caption: Cosine and arccosine across y = x
items.text: The same construction on a different interval. Cosine is cut to [0, π], where it falls steadily from 1 to −1, and the reflection of that piece is arccosine. Note the outputs now run from 0 to π rather than either side of zero.

items.caption: Tangent and arctangent across y = x
items.text: Reflection exchanges the asymptotes too. Tangent's vertical asymptotes at ±π/2 become arctangent's horizontal ones, which is why arctangent accepts every real number and still never reaches ±π/2.

items.secTitle: Compositions of Trigonometric and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
items.caption: 5π/6 in, π/6 out
items.text: Sine sends both angles to the same value, so arcsine cannot tell them apart — and by definition it answers with the one inside its own range. The input is not recovered; it is folded back.

items.caption: What each inverse takes and gives
items.text: Read the horizontal bar as what goes in and the vertical bar as what comes out. Each is the reverse of its parent function's pair, which is the whole content of the word inverse.

items.caption: One period of y = sin x is 2π
items.text: The stretch of curve from 0 to 2π is one complete cycle, and every later stretch of the same length is an exact copy: that is what sin(θ + 2π) = sin θ says. The marker at 60° would read the same 0.866 at 420°, at 780°, and at −300°. Move the marker by a full period and watch the value repeat on the

items.caption: sin(−θ) = −sin θ: P reflected to P′
items.text: Turning by −θ instead of θ reflects the point P across the x-axis to P′: the x-coordinate is unchanged, so cosine is even, and the y-coordinate flips sign, so sine is odd. The two heights marked in the picture are equal and opposite, which is the identity read off the circle rather than proved. Step through the reflection for any angle on the

items.caption: Inside the strip, and never inside it
items.text: The shaded strip is every value from −1 to 1. Sine never leaves it; secant never enters it, touching its edge only at the points where cosine is ±1. That is why sin x = 1.5 and sec x = 0.5 are both impossible, for opposite reasons.

items.caption: y = tan x: a break at every odd multiple of π/2
items.text: The curve is smooth inside each branch, but at π/2, 3π/2 and every odd multiple of π/2 it runs off to infinity on one side and comes back from minus infinity on the other: a vertical asymptote wherever the cosine in the denominator is zero. Sine and cosine themselves have no such breaks because they are coordinates, never quotients. Trace a branch up to its asymptote on the

items.caption: One interval each, chosen for a reason
items.text: Each highlighted stretch is where the function moves in one direction only and still takes every value it ever takes. Those are the exact intervals the inverse functions are built on — which is why the choice is not arbitrary.

items.secTitle: Naming the Sides: Opposite, Adjacent, Hypotenuse
items.caption: The same triangle, the other angle chosen
items.text: Nothing about the triangle changes between these two pictures — only which acute angle is under consideration. The two legs trade the names opposite and adjacent; the hypotenuse keeps its name, because it is defined against the right angle rather than against θ.

items.caption: 30-60-90: sides in the ratio 1 : √3 : 2
items.text: The shortest side faces the 30.0° angle and is half the hypotenuse; the side facing 60.0° is √3 ≈ 1.732 times the shortest. Those two facts are the whole of the exact-value table for 30° and 60°: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, and the same numbers swapped at 60°. items.text: Measured from θ the vertical leg is the opposite side; measured from 90° − θ the same leg is the adjacent side. Both readings divide it by the same hypotenuse, which is why sin θ and cos(90° − θ) are the same number.

items.caption: One line of sight, two observers
items.text: The two horizontals are parallel and the line of sight cuts both, so the angle measured upward from below and the angle measured downward from above are alternate interior angles. They are equal, which means either end of the problem can be used to set it up.

items.text: Push θ toward either limit and a leg disappears. At 0° the opposite side has no length and at 90° the adjacent side has none — and a ratio with a vanished side in it stops meaning anything, which is where the triangle definitions run out.

items.caption: The same b and A, three lengths of a
items.text: Side b and angle A are identical in all three panels; only the swung side a changes. Where its arc meets the base is where the third vertex can go — twice when a is longer than the height but shorter than b, once when it exactly equals the height, and nowhere when it falls short.

items.text: The side c is computed from the two sides that enclose the angle C and from cos C; when C is a right angle the correction term vanishes and the statement is the Pythagorean theorem. items.secTitle: Area of a Triangle Using Trigonometry
items.caption: The height, written with a sine
items.text: Drop the altitude onto side a and it is the side opposite angle C in a small right triangle whose hypotenuse is b — so its length is b sin C. Half the base times that height is the ordinary area formula with nothing new in it.

items.caption: The same angle on two circles
items.text: Both triangles have the same shape because the angle is the same; only the size differs. On the larger circle every ratio still has to be divided by the radius. Shrink the radius to 1 and the division disappears — the two legs of the triangle simply are the cosine and the sine.

items.caption: 45° and −315°: one terminal side
items.text: The solid blue arc reaches the terminal side by turning 45° counterclockwise; the dashed purple arc reaches the same ray by turning 315° the other way. items.caption: Sine paired with its curve, frozen at 50°
items.text: The vertical leg of the unit-circle triangle IS the sine; the curve on the right tracks it as the ray turns.

items.caption: Cosine paired with its curve, frozen at 50°
items.text: The horizontal leg IS the cosine; the curve on the right follows the x-projection of the moving point.

items.caption: Tangent paired with its curve, frozen at 50°
items.text: Tangent is the ratio of the legs — vertical over horizontal — with asymptotes wherever the horizontal leg vanishes.

items.caption: Cosecant paired with its curve, frozen at 50°
items.text: Cosecant flips the vertical leg into its reciprocal: U-branches blowing up wherever sine shrinks to zero.

items.caption: Secant paired with its curve, frozen at 50°
items.text: Secant flips the horizontal leg: the same U-branch architecture, with poles at cosine’s zeros.

items.caption: Cotangent paired with its curve, frozen at 50°
items.text: Cotangent is horizontal over vertical — tangent inverted, falling where tangent climbs.

items.caption: Sine — Step 1: the angle placed
items.text: The ray parks at 50°: circle on the left, the sine graph on the right, nothing highlighted yet.

items.secTitle: Sine, Step 2: Drop the Vertical Leg
items.caption: Sine — Step 2: the leg highlighted
items.text: The vertical leg lights up on the circle — the geometric quantity that IS sin θ.

items.secTitle: Sine, Step 3: Trace on the Graph
items.caption: Sine — Step 3: pinned to the graph
items.text: The tracking dot pins the graph at θ = 50°, tying the circle reading to the curve.

items.caption: Sine — Step 4: reference angle at 140°
items.text: At 140° the reference-angle arc shows the same magnitude — the quadrant alone decides the sign.

items.caption: Sine — Step 5: one turn later
items.text: At 410° the spiral overlays the 50° ghost: one full turn later, the value returns exactly.

svgs: <svg width="336" height="240" viewBox="0 0 420 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto"><rect x="26" y="26" width="368" height="248" rx="14" fill="#fff" stroke="#e2e8f0"/><rect x="44" y="44" width="332" height="34" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0"/><text x="210" y="61" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="15" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">sec(α/2) = √(2/(1 + cos α))</text><text x="128" y="126" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">sec(α/2) =</text><text x="140" y="126" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">1 / cos(α/2)</text><text x="372" y="141" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="10" fill="#94a3b8" font-family="Georgia,serif">definition</text><text x="128" y="160" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">=</text><text x="140" y="160" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">1 / √((1 + cos α)/2)</text><text x="372" y="175" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="10" fill="#94a3b8" font-family="Georgia,serif">substitute the cos half-angle identity</text><text x="128" y="194" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">=</text><text x="140" y="194" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">√( 2 / (1 + cos α) )</text><text x="372" y="209" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="10" fill="#94a3b8" font-family="Georgia,serif">invert under the root</text></svg>

items.caption: cot(α/2), derived
items.text: The tangent formula flipped: the fraction under the radical turns upside down.
svgs: <svg width="336" height="240" viewBox="0 0 420 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto"><rect x="26" y="26" width="368" height="248" rx="14" fill="#fff" stroke="#e2e8f0"/><rect x="44" y="44" width="332" height="34" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0"/><text x="210" y="61" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="15" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">cot(α/2) = √((1 + cos α)/(1 − cos α))</text><text x="128" y="126" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">cot(α/2) =</text><text x="140" y="126" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">1 / tan(α/2)</text><text x="372" y="141" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="10" fill="#94a3b8" font-family="Georgia,serif">definition</text><text x="128" y="160" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">=</text><text x="140" y="160" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">1 / √((1 − cos α)/(1 + cos α))</text><text x="372" y="175" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="10" fill="#94a3b8" font-family="Georgia,serif">substitute the tan half-angle identity</text><text x="128" y="194" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">=</text><text x="140" y="194" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="14" fill="#1e3a5f" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic">√( (1 + cos α) / (1 − cos α) )</text><text x="372" y="209" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="central" font-size="10" fill="#94a3b8" font-family="Georgia,serif">invert under the root</text></svg>

items.caption: y = sin θ, frozen at θ = 60°
items.text: The bounded wave between −1 and 1; the marker rides at 60°, where sin θ = √3/2 ≈ 0.866.

items.caption: y = cos θ, frozen at θ = 60°
items.text: The same wave started from its maximum at θ = 0; at the marker, cos θ = 1/2 exactly.

items.caption: y = tan θ, frozen at θ = 60°
items.text: Climbing branches fenced by asymptotes π apart; at the marker, tan θ = √3 ≈ 1.732.

items.caption: y = csc θ, frozen at θ = 60°
items.text: U-branches opening away from the axis, asymptotes standing at sine’s zeros; the marker reads csc θ ≈ 1.155.

items.caption: y = sec θ, frozen at θ = 60°
items.text: The same U-branch architecture positioned over the cosine wave; at the marker, sec θ = 2 exactly.

items.caption: y = cot θ, frozen at θ = 60°
items.text: Strictly falling branches interlocking with tangent’s; the marker reads cot θ = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577.

items.caption: y = sin x, the baseline state
items.text: Every parameter at its neutral value: amplitude 1, period 2π, no shift, midline on the x-axis. The four annotations name the four features the sliders move.

items.caption: A = 3, everything else unchanged
items.text: The red bracket measures 3 and the dots read max = 3, min = −3. The period bracket and the crossings sit exactly where they did at A = 1, because A acts outside the function.

items.caption: A = −2, with the positive wave dashed behind it
items.text: The solid curve is the dashed one mirrored in the midline. The maximum and minimum dots have traded places, and the amplitude readout stays at |A| = 2, because a distance is never negative.

items.caption: B = 2, the period halved
items.text: One cycle now spans π instead of 2π, so two cycles fill the interval that held one. The amplitude bracket is the same length as before: an inside factor rescales the horizontal axis only.

items.caption: B = 2 and C = π, so the shift is π/2
items.text: The equation carries C = π while the violet bar measures π/2. The standard cycle begins where Bx − C = 0, which is x = C/B — the division by B is the step most often skipped.

items.caption: D = 2, the midline lifted
items.text: The dashed midline has moved to y = 2 and carried the maximum and minimum with it, to 3 and 1. The amplitude bracket has not changed length, which is how you tell a lift from a stretch.

items.caption: y = 2 sin(2x − π) + 1
items.text: All four parameters away from neutral at once. Each annotation still reports one parameter: amplitude 2, period π, shift π/2, midline 1, with the peak at 3 and the trough at −1.

items.caption: y = tan x, the unbounded case
items.text: No amplitude bracket and no maximum or minimum dots, because the branches run to infinity between the dashed asymptotes. The period bracket survives and spans π, half the sine and cosine value.

items.caption: Step 1: y = 1/2 against the full sine curve
items.text: The dashed red line meets the curve at several points in view, and infinitely many overall. Each crossing is a different x with the same output, so no single answer exists for “which x gives 1/2”.

items.caption: Step 3: sine kept on [−π/2, π/2], then reflected
items.text: The blue piece is sine on its principal interval; the amber curve is its mirror image in y = x, which is arcsin. Its domain is [−1, 1] and its range is [−π/2, π/2] — the kept piece with the axes swapped.

items.caption: Step 3: cosine kept on [0, π], then reflected
items.text: Cosine needs a different cut: [0, π], where it falls steadily from 1 to −1. The amber reflection is arccos, defined on [−1, 1] and returning angles in [0, π].

items.caption: Step 3: tangent kept on (−π/2, π/2), then reflected
items.text: The dashed vertical asymptotes of tangent reflect into horizontal ones. Arctan is defined for every real input and never quite reaches −π/2 or π/2.

items.caption: Step 4: arcsin(sin(5π/6))
items.text: The input 5π/6 lies outside the shaded principal interval. sin(5π/6) = 1/2, and arcsin returns the one angle inside the interval with that value, π/6. The composition folds the input back instead of undoing sine.

items.caption: Equilateral, frozen
items.text: Three equal sides force three equal angles — 60° each, the only split of 180° into three equal parts.
